2FA: Does Not Identify the Device When you setup 2FA for some of your accounts, everytime you login into some platform, the message you get is "Identify Your Device", which send some numeric code to verify. But the truth is that, what QR code or Authority Keys do, is that they identify the code that was generated by the QR code identification, not the device. So, if you delete your account from your device, and setup the same device with the same account, your Authority 2FA will not work anymore, because it doesn't identify Your device, but that random code generated in the moment you can the QR code. This is not security, this is false security. Useful but false. What the QR code actually contains A secret, encoded in a format that the application knows how to read. That secret is combined with the current time to produce six digits, and the same calculation is repeated on the server. If the two numbers match, the login is accepted. There is no fingerprint of the phone in that calculation, and there is no name of the person. The code proves that the device holds the secret, not that the device is yours. Why deleting the account breaks everything When the account is removed from the application, the secret is removed with it. The phone is the same, the user is the same, the number of the SIM is the same, but the thing that produced the six digits is gone. Setting the account up again generates a new secret, and the server replaces the old one, which is why the old codes no longer work. From the outside this looks like a device problem. From the inside it is a secret problem, and the difference matters: a device can be recognised, a secret can only be known. The word the screen should use "Identify your device" is a promise the protocol never made. It identifies a shared secret, which is a much smaller claim, and a much more honest one. The protection is real, in the sense that a password stolen from a database is not enough anymore, but it is protection against a copy of the password, not against a person who has your phone. Useful but false, as the title says. I still use it, because useful and imperfect is better than perfect and absent.
3wiseMonkeys: Why Refusing to (See, Listen or Speak "Evil") can be positive? 2026-05-24 — — First Lesson: Learn to Deny Orders . Accept suggestions, Accept Critics, Deny Orders! Second Lesson: You are Free . You can make a Choice . Third Lesson: Your Mindset and Your Will to change, is the Key to archive any gold. The image everybody knows and nobody reads Three monkeys, one covering his eyes, one covering his ears, one covering his mouth. The image travels around the world as a decoration, printed on small statues and sold in airports, and almost always it is read as a lesson in obedience: do not see evil, do not hear evil, do not speak evil. Be quiet, be useful, and let the world happen to somebody else. That reading never convinced me. A monkey with his hands over his eyes is not blind, he is choosing. The gesture is active. It says: this, for now, does not enter. And a choice about what enters the mind is the first form of discipline that any person can practice, because attention is the only door we can close without asking permission. To see everything is to be at the mercy of everything A mind that cannot close a door is not open, it is unprotected. The endless feed, the notification, the argument of a stranger at three in the morning, the news that repeats itself every hour with a new face: none of it asks whether we have room for it. It simply arrives, and the mind that says yes to everything ends up owned by everything. So the first monkey is not refusing knowledge. He is refusing noise, which is a different substance. Knowledge has a shape, a source and a reason to exist. Noise has an urgency. Learning to tell them apart takes years and it is the most profitable skill I know. Orders and suggestions are not the same thing A suggestion offers a reason and leaves the decision with me. A critic offers a correction and leaves the decision with me. An order removes the decision, and a person who only follows orders never learns to judge, because judgement is the exact part that was taken away. This is why the first lesson is about refusing without guilt. I am not telling anyone to be rude to a teacher, a parent or a boss. I am saying that the sentence do it because I say so is the sentence that makes a person replaceable. The ability to say no to an order is the same ability that lets someone say no to a bad idea, and a society of people who cannot refuse is a society that can be pointed anywhere by whoever speaks loudest. Accept the suggestion, consider the critic, refuse the order. In that order, every time. Not because authority is always wrong, but because authority without a reason is not authority yet, it is only volume. Freedom is a verb with a price Freedom is not the absence of limits. It is the presence of a choice, which implies that there is more than one path and that the person is the one who walks. Without that, freedom is only a word used in speeches, and the speeches are usually written by people who would prefer that we did not use it. The second monkey covers his ears because some voices are not offering a path, they are offering a direction. A direction comes with a promised reward: the correct opinion, the correct career, the correct life. A path comes with work. The difference is not in the volume of the voice, it is in whether the voice survives the question why . The third monkey, and the gold that is not money The third one covers his mouth, and people read it as silence before injustice. I read it as economy. Words spent on what cannot be changed are words taken from what can. The mouth is not sealed, it is reserved for the sentence that deserves to exist. The gold of the third lesson is not money. It is whatever a person builds when nobody is deciding for him: a habit, a craft, a text, a family, a piece of software, a garden. The mindset is the key, the will is the hand that turns it, and the door opens on the other side of the noise that the three monkeys decided to ignore. How to practice it this week Nothing here works as a theory. It works as a repetition, and it is small enough to start today: Pick one source of noise and close it for seven days. Not forever. Seven days. When someone gives you an order, ask for the reason. If the reason exists, follow it with more will than before. When someone gives you a label, wait a day before accepting it. Labels age badly. Choose one thing to build that nobody asked for, and give it twenty minutes a day. That is the whole discipline. The monkey does not refuse the world. He refuses to be carried by it, and in that small distance between the world and the mind there is room enough for a life. ↑

ArmedViolence: Skip to document AOV Dossier Sections Research dossier · Revised 21 October 2026 The Arithmetic of Armed Violence A documented accounting of how many people are killed by firearms and explosives — by civilians, police, soldiers, and children — and an evidence-based argument that weapons are not instruments of solution. It closes with the methods that measurably do work. 0 U.S. firearm deaths, 2024 [2] 0 Global firearm deaths per year (GBD) [1] 0 Explosive-weapon casualties reported, 2024 [12] 0 Share of those 2024 bomb casualties who were civilians [12] Figures are reported exactly as their sources report them, with the year and the dataset named. Where a number is modelled, estimated, or incomplete, this document says so. 00 — Abstract What this document argues, and what it does not This dossier rests on a premise stated plainly: a gun is always a bad tool. That is a moral claim, and no table of figures can prove a moral claim. What the figures can do is something narrower and more useful: they can show what the tool actually produces when it is used, at scale, by every kind of person who uses it. So the document proceeds in two movements. First, an accounting. We count the dead by category — homicide, suicide, accident, police action, war, bombing — and by the hand that held the weapon: a civilian, an officer, a soldier, a child. Second, an argument. From that accounting we ask a practical question: does the weapon solve the problem it was produced to solve? The evidence assembled here says no, and says it consistently enough that the burden of proof has shifted. A third movement follows, because criticism without construction is cheap. If weapons do not solve conflicts between persons, what does? Here the literature is unusually clear and unusually ignored: organised nonviolence outperforms armed struggle by roughly two to one; street-level violence interruption has cut shootings in specific neighbourhoods by double-digit percentages; restorative conferencing measurably reduces repeat offending; purchaser licensing is associated with large reductions in firearm homicide. We report those, including the places where the evidence is weak. A note on intellectual honesty This is an advocacy document built on real data, and it says so. Where a widely-cited claim turned out to be unsupported — gun buybacks, for instance, or the idea that hospital-based violence intervention is a proven fix for adults — the claim is marked as unsupported rather than quietly dropped. An argument that only works when inconvenient evidence is hidden is not an argument. It is advertising. 01 — Method & definitions How the numbers were assembled Four rules governed the collection of every figure in this document. Every number carries its year and its dataset. A death count without a year is not a fact; it is a rumour with a comma in it. "44,447" means nothing until it is labelled CDC/NVSS, 2024, United States . Modelled estimates are labelled as models. The global figures in this document come from the Global Burden of Disease study, which estimates deaths where civil registration is incomplete. They are the best available global figures. They are not censuses, and they carry uncertainty intervals that this document reports. Casualties are not deaths. Bombing datasets usually count people killed and injured. Mixing the two produces inflated headlines, so each table below states which measure it uses. Different datasets are not interchangeable. Where two credible sources disagree — and on conflict deaths they do — both are shown rather than reconciled by force. Firearm death A death where a gunshot wound is the underlying cause, recorded by intent: homicide, suicide, unintentional, legal intervention, or undetermined. Explosive violence Harm from manufactured explosives — bombs, shells, grenades, mines, cluster munitions — as distinct from gunfire. Casualty One person killed or injured. Used only where the source does not separate the two, and flagged when so. Civilian A person not taking direct part in hostilities. Explosive-weapon datasets count civilians specifically because they dominate the toll. 02 — The global ledger A quarter of a million people, every year The most complete global breakdown of firearm deaths by intent comes from the Global Burden of Disease study covering 1990–2016. It puts the annual worldwide total at 251,000 firearm deaths, within an uncertainty interval of 195,000 to 276,000. Global firearm deaths by intent, 2016 (GBD modelled estimate) [1] Intent Deaths Uncertainty interval Share Homicide 161,000 107,000–182,000 64% Suicide 67,500 55,400–84,100 27% Unintentional 23,000 18,200–24,800 9% Total 251,000 195,000–276,000 100% Rounded as published; categories need not sum exactly to the reported total. Uncertainty intervals are the study's own. Homicide 161,000 Suicide 67,500 Unintentional 23,000 Two things about that table matter more than the total. The first is the suicide share: roughly one in four firearm deaths worldwide, and in the United States more than six in ten, is a person killing themselves. A weapon kept for protection is, statistically, far more likely to be used against its owner than against an intruder. The second is the homicide share. Two-thirds of the global toll is people killing other people — not states killing enemies, not soldiers killing soldiers, but ordinary homicide. Wider violent death The Small Arms Survey's Global Violent Deaths database counts intentional homicide, direct conflict deaths, and killings during legal intervention, and deliberately excludes suicide. Its 2022 update recorded 531,000 violent deaths in 2020, of which 211,000 were firearm deaths . A subsequent report describes approximately 580,000 violent deaths in 2021 , of which about 45% were inflicted with firearms. [4] [5] Read against the GBD figure, the implication is uncomfortable and worth stating directly: firearms are not one hazard among many. They are the single mechanism through which a very large share of the world's intentional killing is done. Wars, and the soldiers in them The military is the category in which the weapon is most formally justified: the state issues it, trains the holder, and directs its use toward a declared enemy. It is also the category with the largest single-event totals in human history. The Uppsala Conflict Data Program recorded 154,000 deaths from organised violence worldwide in 2023 , down from 310,000 in 2022 — a measure broader than state-based war deaths alone, which also counted 20,900 deaths in non-state conflicts in 2023. For 2024 Uppsala reports nearly 160,000 deaths in organised violence , including roughly 76,000 battle-related deaths in Ukraine and about 26,000 across the Israel–Gaza and Hezbollah–Lebanon conflicts , of which 94% were civilians or people of unknown identity . [39] [40] Recent conflict mortality, by dataset and scope — these series are not interchangeable [39] [40] [41] Measure Year Deaths Dataset Battle-related deaths 2023 >122,000 PRIO / UCDP overview State-based conflict deaths 2023 138,917 UCDP GED, via Our World in Data State-based conflict deaths 2024 155,038 UCDP GED, via Our World in Data Organised violence, all forms 2024 ≈160,000 UCDP The two 2023 figures differ because they are different products from the same research programme; the sources available do not reconcile them, so both are shown. Uppsala's 2024 organised-violence total is broader than battle deaths alone and must not be substituted for that measure. Zoom out, and the same pattern holds at civilisational scale. World War II killed an estimated 70–85 million people . One widely used museum estimate divides that as 15 million battle deaths and 45 million civilian deaths — civilians at roughly 75% of the listed total. The museum cautions that estimates vary widely and that civilian deaths in China alone may have exceeded 50 million, so this is a source-specific estimate rather than a settled ratio. [42] [43] Read those two paragraphs together and a striking thing appears. The category where weapons are most organised, most professionalised, and most heavily regulated is also the category where the people killed are least likely to be the people holding the weapons. The soldier's weapon does not mainly kill soldiers. It kills the people who live where the fighting happens. “About one in two homicides globally involves a firearm.” WHO, Global Status Report on Violence Prevention, on 475,000 homicides in 2012 [3] 03 — The United States The richest country, and its ledger The United States is the most completely documented case in the world, because it counts its dead through a national vital registration system rather than a model. In 2024 it recorded 44,447 firearm deaths — 13.1 per 100,000 people. [2] U.S. firearm deaths by intent, 2024 (CDC/NVSS, tabulated by Pew Research Center) [2] Intent Deaths Share Suicide 27,593 62.1% Homicide 15,364 34.6% Legal intervention 636 1.4% Accidental 450 1.0% Undetermined 404 0.9% Total 44,447 100% The official CDC/NCHS FastStats page publishes the total and rate; the intent breakdown above is Pew's tabulation of the same CDC mortality data. The categories sum to the reported total. 0 people killed by a firearm in the United States on an average day in 2024. One every twelve minutes. 0 of those daily deaths, on average, are suicides — a person using a gun on themselves. 0 are homicides. The remainder are accidents, police action, and undetermined deaths. The suicide majority is the argument Most public argument about guns concerns homicide, because homicide is what appears in the news. The data says the weapon's primary human output is different. Sixty-two percent of American firearm deaths are suicides. And suicide is, uniquely among these categories, a problem where the method determines the outcome: the difference between a suicide attempt with a firearm and an attempt by most other means is largely a difference between dying and surviving. That is why the American toll is not primarily a story about crime. It is a story about a household object that converts a transient crisis into a permanent outcome. The person who dies is, in the overwhelming majority of cases, the person who owns the gun or lives with whoever does. Police killings The state's own use of firearms is a documented category, not an abstraction. Because no comprehensive federal database existed for decades, two independent projects filled the gap. Mapping Police Violence recorded 1,365 people killed by police in 2024 and 1,314 in 2025 — all fatal encounters, including shootings, tasers, physical force and vehicles, not shootings alone. The Washington Post's Fatal Force database counted 10,429 fatal police shootings across 2015–2024 . [6] [7] These are lawful killings, in the main, carried out by people authorised to carry weapons and trained in their use. They belong in the ledger precisely because they complicate the premise that a gun in trained hands is a categorically different thing from a gun in untrained hands. The same instrument produces the same outcome; only the paperwork differs. 04 — The smallest hands Children, on both ends of the weapon In 2021, 2,571 children aged 1–17 died from firearms in the United States — a rate of 3.7 per 100,000. Across ages 1–19 the count was 4,733 , and firearms accounted for 20% of all deaths in that age group , against an average of less than 2% in comparably large and wealthy peer nations. [8] The same KFF analysis found that the U.S. firearm death rate for ages 1–19 was more than 9.5 times that of Canada, the peer country with the next-highest rate. That comparison uses U.S. data for 2021 and peer data for 2019, which is worth knowing before quoting it. The trend is not ambiguous. Pew's analysis of CDC data recorded 1,732 firearm deaths among Americans under 18 in 2019 , rising to 2,590 in 2021 — a roughly 50% increase in two years. [9] School shootings with casualties, K–12, per Education Week's definition [10] Year Incidents Killed Injured 2022 51 40 100 2023 38 21 42 2024 39 18 59 Education Week counts only incidents where a person other than the shooter was injured by gunfire on K–12 school property during school hours or a school event, and excludes suicides. Other trackers use broader definitions and therefore report larger numbers. Beyond the United States, children are killed and maimed as a direct instrument of war. The United Nations verified 5,301 children killed and 11,649 killed or maimed in armed conflict in 2023. In 2024 it verified 11,967 children killed or maimed . Between 2005 and 2022 the UN verified more than 120,000 children killed or maimed in conflict. [15] [16] Children are also the ones who find the weapon at home. The category the CDC labels “unintentional” is small in absolute terms — 450 deaths in 2024 — and disproportionately young. A tool designed to be lethal at a distance does not distinguish between an intended target and a four-year-old in the next room. “Firearms accounted for one in five deaths among Americans aged 1–19 — against under one in fifty in peer countries.” KFF analysis of CDC and international data [8] 05 — Explosives When the weapon is a bomb, the victim is a bystander Bombs differ from guns in one decisive respect: they cannot be aimed with precision at a person. They are area weapons, and the area contains whoever happens to be in it. Every serious dataset on explosive violence reflects this, and the trend is worsening. Reported global casualties from explosive weapons, AOAV Explosive Violence Monitor [12] Year Killed & injured Civilians Civilian share 2020 18,747 11,056 59% 2021 19,473 11,102 57% 2022 31,273 20,793 66% 2023 47,476 34,791 73% 2024 67,026 59,524 89% AOAV monitors incidents reported in English-language media, so its totals are a floor, not a census. In its 2024 report, 24,147 civilians were killed and 35,377 injured — those sum to the civilian total. AOAV's later initial data for 2024 retrospectively revised 2023 civilian casualties upward to 36,640; report editions are snapshots, not a fixed series. 2020 18,747 2021 19,473 2022 31,273 2023 47,476 2024 67,026 Casualties from explosive weapons roughly tripled in five years, and the civilian share climbed from 59% to 89%. This is not a coincidence of two independent trends. It is what happens when area weapons are used in populated places. The United Nations puts the general figure at about 90% of casualties being civilians when explosive weapons are used in populated areas, against about 10% elsewhere. The ICRC makes the same point about urban warfare: civilians are an estimated 90% of casualties when wars are fought in cities. [17] [18] Mines and explosive remnants Explosive weapons also kill after the fighting stops, which no firearm does. Landmine Monitor recorded 5,757 casualties in 2023 — 1,983 killed, 3,663 injured, 111 with status unknown. Civilians were 4,335, or 84% of casualties where civilian or military status was known, and 1,498 of them were children , 37% of civilian casualties where age was recorded. The 2025 edition reports 6,279 casualties . [13] The 2022 figures were 4,710 casualties, 85% civilian, with about half of civilian casualties being children. The direction of travel is upward, and the victims are not combatants. Three documented cases Hiroshima & Nagasaki, 1945 66,000 dead in Hiroshima 39,000 dead in Nagasaki The Manhattan Engineer District's 1946 report gives these as the best available figures, with 69,000 and 25,000 injured respectively, and explicitly warns that estimates are discrepant. [14] Oklahoma City, 19 April 1995 168 dead, including 19 children A truck bomb outside a federal building. The FBI's case history records 168 dead and several hundred injured, in a building that housed a day-care centre. [19] September 11, 2001 2,977 dead Four hijacked aircraft used as guided weapons. The figure is the victim toll, excluding the 19 hijackers. [20] Three cases, three technologies, one structural feature: in each, the people killed were not the people with whom the perpetrator had a dispute. A bomb is a tool for converting a grievance into the deaths of strangers. That is what it is for . There is no version of the device that does something else. 06 — The defensive claim The one argument that would matter, and what it shows The strongest available defence of the weapon is not that it is pleasant, but that it is necessary: that a good person with a gun stops a bad person with a gun. This is the only claim that could rescue the tool from the ledger above. So it deserves the most careful examination in the document. The FBI studied 160 active-shooter incidents between 2000 and 2013, in which 486 people were killed and 557 wounded, excluding shooters. In 21 incidents — 13.1% — unarmed citizens successfully restrained the shooter . [21] RAND's analysis goes further into the mechanics. Bystanders or security personnel attempted to intervene in 65 cases. Of those interventions, 44 ended the shooting, 12 were partly successful, and 9 failed. Among the 56 successful or partly successful interventions, 45 — 80% — did not involve armed defence at all . RAND identified only two cases in which civilian bystanders used firearms to stop a shooter; most of the eleven cases where gunfire stopped a shooter involved security guards or off-duty officers. [22] 45 / 56 successful or partly successful interventions that involved no armed defence 2 cases in which a civilian bystander used a firearm to stop a shooter 13.1% of 160 FBI active-shooter incidents stopped by unarmed citizens These findings do not prove that an armed bystander can never help; that would be a stronger claim than the data supports. What they show is that the scenario at the centre of the armed-defence argument — the armed civilian who saves the day — is rare, while the unarmed intervention is comparatively common. The tool's advertised purpose is not its observed function. And the costs are not symmetrical. A weapon present in a confrontation raises the probability that the confrontation becomes lethal, whoever is holding it, and it does so in every category this document has counted: the domestic argument, the suicidal crisis, the police stop, the school hallway, the crowded street. The benefit is a rare, conditional good. The cost is an actuarial certainty. Evidence quality note RAND's intervention cases are selected from incidents in which someone chose to intervene, and the FBI's active-shooter category excludes gang- and drug-related shootings. Neither dataset is a controlled comparison of armed versus unarmed response, and no such experiment could ethically be run. Readers should treat this section as the best available observational evidence, not as a decisive causal result. 07 — Why the tool fails Five structural reasons a weapon cannot solve a problem The figures above are a symptom. The argument is about mechanism. A weapon fails as a problem-solving instrument not because it is used badly, but because of what it is. 01 It addresses the person, not the problem Every human conflict has a structure: a disputed resource, a broken agreement, a wounded standing, a fear about the future. A weapon can remove a participant. It cannot remove any of those. The dispute survives the person, usually with more participants and less trust. 02 It is irreversible, and it is used in irreversible moments The 27,593 American firearm suicides in 2024 are the clearest evidence. A decision made in a crisis of minutes becomes permanent because the method allows no interval for reconsideration. A tool whose defining property is that it cannot be taken back is a poor instrument for resolving situations that change. 03 It cannot discriminate, and it is used where discrimination is everything Firearms miss. Explosives do not aim. In populated areas, the UN estimate is that 90% of casualties from explosive weapons are civilians. A tool that cannot reliably tell

BestSuperDumb_1: FreeBSD Basics: Some notes Add New User Account useradd Remove Old User Account rmuser username Update information about user (including pass) chpass username Create new group pw groupadd groupname Add user to new group pw groupmod groupname -M user Main Folders for Configuration of applications and services /boot/loader.conf /etc/rc.conf /usr/local/ Default editors vi & ee Default shells /bin/sh & /bin/csh One correction before you copy and paste On FreeBSD the interactive way to create an account is adduser , and the scriptable way is pw useradd . The bare useradd belongs to Linux, and it is the habit that most of us bring from there. Two commands, two different systems, and a page of notes is exactly where that difference should be written down. Why these files matter FreeBSD separates what the base system needs from what the packages need, and the separation is visible in the paths. The base lives in /etc , the ports and packages live in /usr/local , and each one has its own place for configuration. /etc/rc.conf is the list of services that start with the machine. One line per service, written by hand, read at boot. No magic tool that rewrites it behind your back, which is a blessing the first time something refuses to start and a curse the first time you forget what you wrote. /boot/loader.conf is the same idea one level lower. What it contains is loaded before the kernel has a chance to ask anything, so a mistake there can leave the machine without a network or without a console. Change one line, reboot, check, then change the next. Small tools, long life vi and ee are not the best editors in the world. They are the ones that will be there when the network is down and the only thing that works is the console. The same is true of /bin/sh and /bin/csh : they are not fashionable, they are present. A BSD guy is dumb in the way a hammer is dumb. It does one thing, it does it the same way every time, and it never asks to be updated before it can hit a nail.

No process is totally isolated while it shares a kernel or a hypervisor with an attacker. What you can build is a sealed cell : one application, one identity, one read-only root, one narrow data path, one network exception, one log stream — and a tested way back. This manual walks from first login to that cell, then shows you where the cell can still leak. Start at zero → Jump to the cell 14 chapters 60+ commands — sources 0 external assets HOST · DEBIAN 13 VM / HYPERVISOR BOUNDARY NAMESPACES · CGROUPS · LSM APP · UID 1001 CELL one job / no ambient authority systemd 257 AppArmor nftables cgroups v2 rootless Podman QEMU/KVM seccomp 00 Level 00 · Orientation · 12 min Field briefing # Isolation is not a product you install. It is a set of boundaries you can name, test and explain. Before you copy a single systemd directive, decide what you are isolating the application from , and what the application must still be able to reach. That answer decides the architecture. ! “Totally isolated” is a direction, not a checkbox. A container shares the host kernel. A VM shares the hypervisor. A separate host shares the network and the supply chain. Every layer removes a class of reachability; none removes the need to patch, monitor and recover. The three questions ask these before every directive What can it read? Configuration, credentials, other users' homes, the host's process list, kernel interfaces, the network. Confidentiality What can it write? Its data directory, logs, temporary files, the package database, cron, systemd units, other processes' memory. Integrity What can it reach? Loopback services, the LAN, the internet, the container runtime socket, the D-Bus, the kernel attack surface. Reachability Threat model, without theatre Write down the adversary and the boundary that is supposed to stop it. If the boundary is “the application is well behaved”, you do not have a boundary. The table below is a starting point, not a compliance claim. Adversary Typical entry Boundary that matters What usually fails Compromised dependency Build script, package, npm/pip crate, plugin Dedicated UID + read-only root + egress deny It runs with the app's full data and network reach Remote attacker Exposed service, weak auth, deserialisation Default-deny firewall + minimal service + patch cadence One forgotten port, one shared admin password Malicious local user Shell on the host, stolen key, sudo mistake Unix permissions + namespaces + audit trail World-writable paths, broad sudo, readable secrets Insider / operator error Wrong mount, copied unit, chmod 777 Immutable infrastructure + review + backups “Temporary” exceptions that never expire Kernel or hypervisor exploit Container escape, bug in a shared subsystem VM boundary + patched kernel + least privilege Assuming a container is a security boundary Supply-chain host Compromised mirror, image, update channel Signed packages + digest pinning + offline verification Blind curl | bash and floating tags The isolation ladder interactive Each rung is a real boundary with a real cost. Most production cells sit at rung 2 or 3; a hostile workload belongs at rung 4 or 5. Click a rung to see what it buys, what it costs, and where it still leaks. The cell contract seven properties One application One primary process, one job. No shell, no package manager, no compiler, no second daemon unless it is part of the same trust boundary. One identity A dedicated system UID/GID. No shared www-data or docker group. No sudo. No login shell. One writable path State lives in one directory. The root filesystem is read-only. Temporary files die with the process. One network story No network, loopback only, or a named egress path. “It needs internet” is not an architecture. One log stream stdout/stderr to journald, or one log directory collected by the host. The cell cannot rewrite history elsewhere. One update path Packages from Debian, images pinned by digest, or a rebuilt artifact. No self-updating binary inside the cell. One recovery path A snapshot, a backup, or a rebuild recipe that has been tested. If you cannot restore it, you do not own it. Ten rules that survive fashion Least privilege is a budget. Every permission you grant is a future exploit primitive. Start at zero, add one at a time, write down why. Deny by default. Firewall, filesystem, network families, capabilities, syscalls. Allow lists are shorter to review than deny lists. Read-only by default. A writable root is persistence. A writable data directory is the only thing that should survive a restart. No ambient authority. Environment variables, inherited file descriptors, D-Bus, the runtime socket and the host's SSH agent are all ambient authority. Secrets are files, not flags. Not in ExecStart= , not in Environment= , not in the image layer, not in shell history. The kernel is shared until it is not. Containers are excellent packaging and good isolation, but they are not a VM boundary. Patch the boundary, not only the app. Kernel, systemd, OpenSSH, the container runtime, the hypervisor, the firmware. Logs leave the cell. A compromised cell must not be able to edit the evidence of its own compromise. Test the failure. Kill the service, fill the disk, remove the network, reboot the host. Isolation that only works on the happy path is decoration. Write the exception down. Every ProtectHome=no or --privileged needs an owner, a reason and an expiry date. 01 Level 01 · Access · 18 min First login # The first hour decides whether the next year is recoverable. Install less, encrypt the disk, keep a console session open, create a named administrator, and make the baseline visible before you change anything. “Root and a password” is not an access design. Before the first prompt installer decisions Minimal, no desktop For a server cell, install the base system and OpenSSH only. Every extra package is another update stream and another parser exposed to the network. Encrypted root LUKS protects data at rest. It does not protect a running system. Keep a recovery key offline and test a boot with it. One admin identity Do not log in as root. Create an operator account, give it sudo, and use a key. Root gets no SSH and no shared password. Console access Know how to reach the VM console or the physical TTY before you touch SSH or nftables. A firewall mistake should not require a rescue ISO. First five commands look before touching hostnamectl ip -brief address ip route ss -tulpn systemctl --failed journalctl -p 3 -b --no-pager Read the output. You are looking for: a hostname you recognise, only the addresses you expect, no unexpected listeners, no failed units, and no repeating error at boot. Save that output; it is your first baseline. Create the operator not root adduser ops usermod -aG sudo ops install -d -m 0700 -o ops -g ops /home/ops/.ssh # On your workstation: ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -a 100 -C "ops@workstation" ssh-copy-id -i ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub ops@server.example.test # Test the new session before closing the old one: ssh -o PreferredAuthentications=publickey ops@server.example.test ! Keep the old session open. Open a second terminal, log in with the key, run sudo -v , then close nothing until the new path is proven. Most “SSH locked me out” stories start with a single session and a reload. Harden SSH without guessing drop-in config Debian reads /etc/ssh/sshd_config and the files in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ . Put local policy in a numbered drop-in so package updates do not fight your edits. sudo install -d -m 0755 /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d sudo tee /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-hardening.conf >/dev/null <<'EOF' PermitRootLogin no PasswordAuthentication no KbdInteractiveAuthentication no PubkeyAuthentication yes AuthenticationMethods publickey AllowUsers ops X11Forwarding no AllowAgentForwarding no AllowTcpForwarding no PermitTunnel no GatewayPorts no MaxAuthTries 3 MaxSessions 2 LoginGraceTime 20 ClientAliveInterval 300 ClientAliveCountMax 2 LogLevel VERBOSE EOF sudo sshd -t sudo systemctl reload ssh sudo sshd -T | grep -E 'permitrootlogin|passwordauthentication|allowusers|maxauthtries' Directive Why What it breaks PermitRootLogin no Removes a known username with unlimited authority from the network. Root-only workflows; use ops + sudo instead. PasswordAuthentication no Passwords are guessable, replayable and shared. Keys are not immortal, but they are auditable. Old clients, emergency access if the key is lost — keep a console path. AllowUsers ops Reduces the account surface even if another user is created later. Automation accounts; add them explicitly or use AllowGroups . AllowTcpForwarding no Stops an SSH account from becoming a general-purpose proxy into the network. Legitimate tunnels; use a dedicated bastion if required. MaxAuthTries 3 Reduces online guessing and noisy logs. Nothing important if keys are used. Sudo, with a paper trail sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/90-ops # ops ALL=(ALL:ALL) ALL # Defaults:ops use_pty # Defaults:ops logfile="/var/log/sudo-ops.log" sudo chmod 0440 /etc/sudoers.d/90-ops sudo visudo -c use_pty prevents a simple background process from surviving the sudo session. The logfile is a second copy of intent; keep it on the host, not inside the cell. Patch and make it automatic sudo apt update sudo apt full-upgrade sudo apt install --no-install-recommends unattended-upgrades apt-listchanges needrestart sudo dpkg-reconfigure -plow unattended-upgrades # Confirm the timer and the effective policy: systemctl status unattended-upgrades --no-pager sudo unattended-upgrade --dry-run --debug 2>&1 | tail -40 i Automatic updates are not automatic safety. They need a reboot for kernel and some library changes, a working mirror, and a rollback plan. needrestart tells you which services still run old libraries; it does not restart them for you unless configured. Write the baseline evidence before opinion sudo install -d -m 0700 /root/baseline { date -u hostnamectl uname -a dpkg-query -W -f='${Package} ${Version}\n' ss -tulpn nft list ruleset 2>/dev/null || true systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled --no-pager } | sudo tee "/root/baseline/$(date -u +%Y%m%dT%H%M%SZ).txt" >/dev/null sudo chmod 0600 /root/baseline/*.txt ls -l /root/baseline Time, DNS and the network story timedatectl set-ntp true timedatectl status resolvectl status # What is this host allowed to reach? Write it down. ip -brief address ip route sudo ss -tulpn Time matters because TLS, logs and audit correlation depend on it. DNS matters because “no network” is a lie if the resolver still leaks queries. Decide both before you build the cell. 02 Level 02 · Operations · 20 min Command survival kit # You do not need five hundred commands. You need twenty that answer four questions: who am I , what is running , what can it reach , and what changed . Everything else is a variation on those. Identity id , getent passwd , getent group , sudo -l , loginctl list-sessions . who Process ps auxf , pstree -ap , systemd-cgls , lsof -p , /proc/<pid>/ . what Reach ss -tulpn , ip route , nft list ruleset , resolvectl status , lsns . where Change journalctl , apt history , dpkg -V , debsums -c , systemctl status . when Packages: know what you installed apt update apt full-upgrade apt policy openssh-server apt list --installed apt-mark showmanual # Which package owns this file? What did this package install? dpkg -S /usr/sbin/sshd dpkg -L openssh-server # Has any file changed since the package was installed? dpkg -V openssh-server debsums -c Task Command Note Full upgrade apt full-upgrade May remove packages; read the plan before saying yes. Why is this installed? apt-mark showmanual Manual packages are your real dependency budget. Pin a version apt-mark hold pkg Debt. Record the reason and a review date. Find config files dpkg-query -W -f='${Conffiles}\n' pkg Useful before editing a package's default. Integrity check dpkg -V Compares installed files with package metadata. Security tracker debsecan --suite trixie Needs network access to fetch data. systemd: the control plane systemctl status cell.service --no-pager systemctl start cell.service systemctl enable --now cell.service systemctl restart cell.service systemctl reload-or-restart cell.service systemctl cat cell.service systemctl edit --full cell.service systemctl daemon-reload systemctl show cell.service -p User -p Group -p ExecStart -p NoNewPrivileges systemctl list-units --type=service --state=running systemctl list-unit-files --state=enabled systemctl --failed systemctl cat shows the unit and its drop-ins in the order systemd reads them. When a directive “does not work”, the usual cause is a later drop-in overriding it. systemctl show is the truth, not the file you remember editing. Logs: read the timeline, not the last line journalctl -u cell.service -f journalctl -u cell.service --since "1 hour ago" --no-pager journalctl -p warning -b --no-pager journalctl -p err..alert --since today --no-pager journalctl -k -b --no-pager journalctl --disk-usage journalctl --verify journalctl -o json-pretty -u cell.service -n 1 i Boot IDs are your friend. -b means this boot, -b -1 the previous one. After a crash, compare journalctl -b -1 -p err with the current boot before you reboot again and destroy the evidence. Network and namespaces: what is actually listening ss -tulpn ss -tan state established ip -brief address ip route ip netns list lsns resolvectl status # Enter a process's network namespace (requires privilege): sudo nsenter -t "$(pgrep -x cell)" -n ss -tulpn Files and privilege: the two audits you run first # Setuid and setgid binaries: a short list is a good list. sudo find / -xdev -type f \( -perm -4000 -o -perm -2000 \) -print # World-writable files and directories without the sticky bit. sudo find / -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -print sudo find / -xdev -type d -perm -0002 ! -perm -1000 -print # File capabilities instead of setuid. sudo getcap -r / 2>/dev/null # Who can sudo, and to what? sudo -l getent group sudo getent group wheel ! Every setuid binary is a small root door. Remove what you do not use, prefer file capabilities with a narrow capability, and never “fix” a permission problem with chmod 777 . A world-writable directory is a place to plant a symlink, a library or a unit file. Things not to do the short list curl … | bash — you are executing a moving target with your privileges. Download, verify a signature or hash, read it, then run it. chmod -R 777 — it turns a permission bug into a persistence mechanism. Copy-paste a unit with --privileged — you have disabled most of the boundaries you are trying to build. Mount the container runtime socket into an untrusted container — that is root on the host with extra steps. Run a database as root — there is no recovery benefit, only a larger blast radius. Expose a service “just for a minute” — scanners do not wait for you to close it. 03 Level 03 · Advanced foundations · 28 min Isolation primitives # The Linux kernel already contains the fences: identities, capabilities, namespaces, cgroups, seccomp and Linux Security Modules. systemd, Podman, bubblewrap and Firejail are different ways to ask the kernel for the same fences. Learn the primitives and the tools stop being magic. The six layers name the boundary Layer Question Primitive Typical tool Identity Who is this process? UID, GID, supplementary groups, capabilities useradd , setpriv , capsh Filesystem What can it see and write? Mount namespace, bind mounts, read-only mounts, permissions, ACLs ProtectSystem= , bwrap , chroot Process What can it see or signal? PID namespace, hidepid , Yama, cgroups PrivateUsers= , ProcSubset= Network What can it reach? Network namespace, nftables, socket families, IP filters PrivateNetwork= , --network=none Kernel Which syscalls and kernel objects? seccomp-bpf, capabilities, LSM, sysctl SystemCallFilter= , AppArmor Hardware What can it touch directly? IOMMU, device cgroups, VM boundary, no device passthrough PrivateDevices= , KVM, VFIO Identity: a UID is the first wall # A system account with no login shell and no home in the usual place. sudo useradd --system --home-dir /var/lib/cell --shell /usr/sbin/nologin cell sudo install -d -m 0750 -o cell -g cell /var/lib/cell id cell getent passwd cell getent group cell # What can the cell user actually do? sudo -u cell -- id sudo -u cell -- sh -c 'test -r /etc/shadow && echo BAD || echo "cannot read shadow"' A dedicated UID stops the application from reading another service's files purely through Unix permissions. It does not stop it from reading world-readable files, and it does not stop it from using a setuid binary if one is reachable. That is why identity is only the first wall. Capabilities: root split into small, sharp pieces Traditional root is all-or-nothing. Capabilities split it. A service that binds port 443 needs CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE , not CAP_SYS_ADMIN . A service that never changes UIDs needs none of the setuid family. Capability What it grants Rule of thumb CAP_NET_BIND_SERVICE Bind ports below 1024 Use a reverse proxy or grant only this one. CAP_NET_RAW Raw sockets, packet capture Almost never needed by an application. danger CAP_DAC_OVERRIDE Bypass file permission checks Equivalent to “read/write anything”. danger CAP_DAC_READ_SEARCH Bypass read/search checks Reads every file. Avoid. CAP_SETUID / CAP_SETGID Change identity Only for supervisors that deliberately drop privileges. CAP_SYS_ADMIN Mounts, namespaces, many kernel operations “New root.” A cell with this is not contained. danger CAP_SYS_PTRACE Debug or read other processes Breaks process isolation. Avoid in production. CAP_CHOWN Change file ownership Rarely needed after startup. capsh --print getpcaps "$(pgrep -x cell)" 2>/dev/null sudo getcap -r / 2>/dev/null # Remove capabilities from a copy, then test it. sudo cp /usr/bin/ping /usr/local/bin/ping-test sudo setcap cap_net_raw+ep /usr/local/bin/ping-test getcap /usr/local/bin/ping-test sudo setcap -r /usr/local/bin/ping-test ! File capabilities are persistent privilege. They survive a service restart and apply to anyone who can execute the file. Prefer systemd's AmbientCapabilities= or CapabilityBoundingSet= for services; use file capabilities only when the binary must be launched outside the unit. Namespaces: separate views of the same kernel Namespace Isolates What it does not isolate User UID/GID mappings, capability scope Kernel vulnerabilities; shared kernel memory Mount Filesystem tree, mounts, propagation A block device you explicitly pass through PID Process IDs and visibility CPU, memory, kernel resources Network Interfaces, routes, ports, firewall The host's network if you add a veth UTS Hostname and domain name Anything else IPC SysV IPC, POSIX message queues Files, sockets, shared memory you bind-mount Cgroup Cgroup namespace view Resource limits themselves Time Monotonic/boot time offsets Wall-clock time and timestamp trust lsns lsns -t net sudo lsns -p "$(pgrep -x cell)" # Inspect a namespace without entering it: sudo readlink /proc/"$(pgrep -x cell)"/ns/net sudo readlink /proc/1/ns/net # Enter only the network namespace: sudo nsenter -t "$(pgrep -x cell)" -n ip -brief address i User namespaces are the gate for rootless containers. They let an unprivileged user become “root” inside a namespace without becoming root on the host. Some hardening profiles disable unprivileged user namespaces because they widen the kernel attack surface. Check your policy before you promise rootless Podman. cgroups v2: limits are part of isolation Namespaces decide what a process can see ; cgroups decide what it can consume . Without limits, a compromised cell can starve the host, fill the disk, or fork until the PID table is exhausted. mount | grep cgroup2 systemd-cgls systemd-cgtop -m systemctl show cell.service -p MemoryCurrent -p MemoryMax -p CPUQuot

Example: queuing, not cheating on a partner, caring for elders. Ethics (Greek ethos = character/habit): the reflective, systematic study and design of those rules. Ethics asks: are our morals justified? Can we do better? Law: the enforceable minimum. Este nível define o problema, os dois tipos de erro e o contrato de leitura do manual. Uma esquadra recebe 40 denúncias por semana. Umas são verdadeiras, outras são equívocos, algumas são instrumentais — alguém a usar a polícia para resolver uma disputa privada. O trabalho começa exactamente onde a intuição falha: em decidir quem merece atenção, quanto dessa atenção é legítima e que indício sobrevive a uma verificação honesta. A tentação é tratar isto como uma questão de carácter: «bons polícias vêem quem é culpado». Não é. É uma questão de desenho de processo — de probabilidades, de sequências, de verificação independente e de limites. E, ao contrário do que o cinema sugere, a maior parte dos erros graves não nasce de maldade. Nasce de um método que nunca foi testado contra a hipótese de o suspeito ser inocente. 0.1 Duas perguntas que parecem a mesma Quase todos os erros de investigação começam numa inversão silenciosa de duas perguntas: Pergunta A — a que interessa ao tribunal P(culpado | indício) Dado este vestígio, este comportamento, esta coincidência, qual é a probabilidade de esta pessoa ter cometido o crime? Pergunta B — a que o laboratório responde P(indício | culpado) Se esta pessoa fosse culpada, qual seria a probabilidade de encontrar este vestígio? São números diferentes. Podem diferir por ordens de grandeza. Confundi-los é o erro estatístico mais frequente em processos penais — e não é um detalhe académico: foi suficiente para condenar pessoas que nunca tinham estado perto do crime. «O perito disse que só uma em cada milhão de pessoas teria este perfil. Mas numa cidade de três milhões, isso significa três pessoas.» 0.2 A matriz que decide tudo Toda a decisão policial — abordar, revistar, deter, acusar — é uma classificação binária aplicada a uma realidade que não se vê. Há quatro resultados possíveis, e dois deles são erros. Não existe sistema que elimine os dois ao mesmo tempo: só existe escolha sobre onde os colocar. Matriz de confusão aplicada à decisão policial Realidade → Decisão ↓ A pessoa é inocente A pessoa é culpada Sinalizada / detida Falso positivo Custos: liberdade, reputação, violência legítima mal aplicada, perda de confiança de toda uma comunidade. Verdadeiro positivo Objectivo legítimo: responsabilização com prova. Não sinalizada / libertada Verdadeiro negativo O sistema deixou em paz quem devia deixar em paz. Falso negativo Custos: impunidade, vitimização repetida, erosão da confiança. Assimetria que não se pode ignorar Os dois erros não custam o mesmo. Um falso positivo usa contra um cidadão todo o poder do Estado — e é irreversível nos anos que consome. Um falso negativo deixa o crime sem resposta, mas não cria uma nova vítima da polícia. Isso não torna o falso negativo aceitável: obriga apenas a reconhecer que a taxa de falsos positivos é o indicador que mais precisa de escrutínio público . 0.3 Porque é que isto falha na vida real Nos processos revistos por tribunais, comissões de inquérito e organizações de exonerados, os mesmos cinco mecanismos reaparecem. Nenhum exige um polícia corrupto. Todos exigem apenas pressão e um processo mal desenhado. 1. Taxa-base ignorada Um indício raro entre inocentes continua a ser comum quando os inocentes são milhões. 2. Visão em túnel A hipótese inicial passa a filtrar o que se recolhe — e o que se descarta. 3. Prova contaminada A expectativa do investigador molda a interpretação do perito, da testemunha e do próprio registo. 4. Confissão fabricada Sob isolamento, exaustão e sugestão, pessoas inocentes confessam — e depois não conseguem desdizer-se. 5. Pressão para fechar Um caso por resolver é um problema institucional; um caso fechado, mesmo errado, parece uma solução. 6. Métricas perversas Se o sucesso é medido por detenções e não por decisões correctas, o sistema aprende a deter mais. 0.4 Nenhuma polícia está imune Este manual usa casos reais de oito países. Nenhum deles é uma acusação a um povo, a uma farda ou a uma nação. É exactamente o contrário: as más decisões são tratadas aqui como iguais entre si — portuguesas, francesas, britânicas, italianas, neerlandesas, espanholas, norte-americanas ou japonesas. A intuição humana trata probabilidades como se fossem opiniões: «é muito provável» quer dizer «estou convencido». O raciocínio probatório exige outra coisa — números que se podem confrontar, taxas que se podem medir e a humildade de perguntar «comparado com o quê?». 1.1 A inversão que arruína inquéritos Um laboratório conclui: «a probabilidade de encontrar este ADN ao acaso é de uma em um milhão». Um relatório policial escreve: «há uma probabilidade de 99,9999 % de o suspeito ser culpado». A segunda frase não decorre da primeira. Falta a taxa-base: quantas pessoas poderiam ter deixado aquele vestígio, e com que frequência este tipo de vestígio aparece em transferências indirectas. Em 1999, no Reino Unido, a pediatra Roy Meadow testemunhou que a probabilidade de duas mortes súbitas numa família «boa» era de uma em 73 milhões. A estatística foi tratada como prova de homicídio. Sally Clark foi condenada; a condenação foi anulada em 2003, depois de a Royal Statistical Society ter criticado publicamente o raciocínio. O erro não estava na peritagem médica sobre as mortes: estava na aritmética do tribunal. Regra operacional Nunca converter um resultado pericial em probabilidade de culpa sem três elementos: a taxa-base da população relevante, a probabilidade de o vestígio aparecer por outra via e a probabilidade de o vestígio não aparecer se a pessoa for culpada . Sem os três, o número é retórica, não prova. 1.2 Sensibilidade, especificidade e o número que falta Qualquer teste — um cão detector, um algoritmo de reconhecimento facial, um agente experiente, um exame de ADN — tem duas qualidades mensuráveis: Sensibilidade (detecção): de todos os culpados, quantos são assinalados. Especificidade : de todos os inocentes, quantos não são assinalados. Nenhuma das duas responde à pergunta do investigador. A que responde é o valor preditivo positivo (VPP): dos assinalados, quantos são realmente culpados. E o VPP depende de algo que o teste não controla: a prevalência do fenómeno na população em que é aplicado. É por isso que o mesmo teste é aceitável numa fronteira e inaceitável numa escola. Consequência prática Se a sua unidade detém 60 pessoas com base num indicador com VPP de 15 %, está a produzir cerca de 51 detenções de inocentes por 9 de culpados. A resposta correcta não é abandonar o indicador: é usá-lo para priorizar verificação, nunca para fundamentar detenção , e medir o VPP em cada contexto antes de o escalar. 1.3 O limiar: onde se corta o sinal Nenhum indicador separa o mundo em dois. O que existe é uma distribuição de comportamentos, vestígios ou pontuações — e um limiar escolhido por alguém. Baixar o limiar aumenta a detecção e multiplica os falsos positivos; subir o limiar poupa inocentes e deixa passar culpados. A decisão é política e ética antes de ser técnica, e deve ser registada como tal. 1.4 O rácio de verosimilhança: a linguagem honesta da prova A forma mais robusta de comunicar o peso de uma prova é o rácio de verosimilhança (LR). Não diz «a probabilidade de culpa é X». Diz quanto é que a prova desloca a balança entre duas hipóteses: LR = P(prova | hipótese da acusação) ÷ P(prova | hipótese da defesa) Um LR de 10 significa: a prova é dez vezes mais provável se a acusação for verdadeira. Não significa que a acusação seja dez vezes mais provável — para isso é preciso combinar o LR com a probabilidade a priori (probabilidade prévia), que é exactamente o que a falácia do Ministério Público ignora. A escala verbal abaixo é a usada, com variantes, em guias forenses europeus; serve para comunicar, não para substituir o número. A tentação é somar indícios fracos: «cinco coincidências, cada uma com 20 % de probabilidade, dão 67 %». Isto só é verdade se as coincidências forem independentes — e, numa investigação, quase nunca são. Se o mesmo polícia recolheu os cinco elementos, se a mesma testemunha os referiu, se todos derivam da mesma conversa ouvida na mesma noite, então não há cinco provas: há uma prova contada cinco vezes. Teste de dependência Para cada par de indícios, pergunte: «se eu soubesse que o primeiro é falso, a probabilidade do segundo mudaria?» Se a resposta for sim, os indícios estão correlacionados. Nesse caso, some com cautela — ou melhor, procure uma fonte independente que não tenha sido exposta à hipótese inicial. 1.6 O que a probabilidade não decide Mesmo uma probabilidade bem calculada não condena ninguém. Em Portugal, a presunção de inocência está consagrada no artigo 32.º, n.º 2, da Constituição, e o processo penal assenta no princípio in dubio pro reo : a dúvida razoável resolve-se a favor do arguido. O padrão não é «mais provável que não»; é «certeza para além da dúvida razoável», avaliada em conjunto e sujeita a contraditório. Isto significa que o trabalho policial pode — e deve — produzir probabilidades, hierarquias de hipóteses e rácios. O que não pode é confundir a sua própria escala interna de suspeita com o padrão jurídico de prova. A fronteira entre as duas é o que separa uma investigação de uma convicção. É essa ligação — e não a aparência — que pode justificar uma abordagem proporcional. 2.2 Concentração: o crime não é uniforme O crime concentra-se. Uma minoria de locais produz a maioria dos incidentes; uma minoria de vítimas sofre a maioria das repetições; e, após um crime, a probabilidade de novo crime no mesmo local e nas semanas seguintes sobe — fenómeno designado near-repeat victimisation . Isto não é uma teoria sobre pessoas: é uma regularidade sobre lugares e tempo, e é testável. AV Dr. Alistair Vance & The Symbiotic Initiative Published October 2026 • Global Epistemology & Technology Review 00 Introduction: The Threshold of Co-Evolution Every major technological revolution in human history has forced a profound renegotiation of what it means to be human. The mastery of fire externalized survival; the printing press democratized cognition; the industrial engine augmented muscle. Today, artificial intelligence stands as the final frontier of tool-making: the externalization and scaling of cognition itself. Yet, public discourse remains gripped by a polarized paralysis—split violently between techno-utopians predicting an imminent paradise of automated leisure and catastrophists invoking deterministic dystopias of existential subjugation. Neither narrative captures reality. Artificial intelligence is neither a benevolent deity nor a rogue demonic entity; it is an algorithmic mirror forged from the cumulative history, data, biases, and brilliance of human civilization. It accelerates whatever dynamics we feed into it. Consequently, asking what AI will do to us is the wrong inquiry. The more urgent, uncomfortable question is: What must humanity fix within itself so that AI can elevate our species rather than automate our decay? 01 Part I: The Mirror of Intelligence When pruned of marketing hype, artificial intelligence offers unprecedented tools for civilizational uplift. By operating at combinatorial speeds impossible for biological neural networks, advanced models function across multiple transformative dimensions: 🧬 Cognitive & Scientific Synthesis Simulating complex biological pathways, protein folding, and material science discoveries in months instead of centuries, effectively compressing medical research timelines. ⚖️ Overcoming Psychological Biases Acting as an objective cognitive partner that challenges confirmation bias, analyzes systemic blind spots, and parses vast datasets free from emotional fatigue. 🕊️ Liberating Human Potential Automating bureaucratic drudgery and mechanical labor to redirect human bandwidth toward interpersonal empathy, philosophical inquiry, and creative expression. By absorbing the collective digital output of humanity, AI becomes an unsparing mirror. It reflects our cultural masterpieces alongside our historical prejudices, forcing us into a vital ontological awakening: to build a wise machine, we must confront the unresolved fractures in our own collective psyche. 02 Part II: The Reality Check Honesty demands that we confront the profound hazards and systemic frictions inherent in current AI trajectories. To romanticize artificial intelligence without acknowledging its structural pathologies is to invite catastrophe. Epistemic Drift and Hallucinations Unlike deterministic calculators, generative models synthesize probabilistic tokens based on patterns. When they invent false citations, logical fallacies, or authoritative falsehoods ("hallucinations"), they exploit human susceptibility to fluent authority—threatening to poison our epistemic commons with synthetic noise. Ecological and Energy Tolls Training and operating frontier foundation models requires staggering amounts of electrical power, specialized semiconductors, and fresh water for data center cooling. In an era of escalating climate crisis, unbridled compute scaling risks compounding ecological degradation unless decoupled from fossil fuels. The Concentration of Power and Moral Outsourcing AI development remains dangerously concentrated within a handful of monopolistic tech conglomerates backed by venture capital. Furthermore, humans increasingly suffer from moral outsourcing —delegating high-stakes judicial, medical, and ethical decisions to opaque algorithms to evade personal responsibility. The Danger of Opaque Agency "When we treat algorithms as infallible oracles rather than statistical instruments, we abdicate our moral duty and risk locking historical biases into immutable digital stone." 03 Part III: What Humans Must Improve to Elevate AI If artificial intelligence is to become a true catalyst for human flourishing rather than an amplifier of our worst impulses, humanity must undergo rigorous internal evolution. The engineering bottleneck is no longer solely in silicon; it is in human wisdom. 1. Epistemic Hygiene & Curation Shifting from gathering gargantuan unvetted datasets to curating high-integrity, ethically rigorous, and diverse knowledge corpora that prioritize truth over engagement metrics. 2. Rewriting Incentives Transitioning from attention-economy algorithms that monetize outrage and division toward alignment metrics that reward societal cohesion, scientific truth, and long-term sustainability. 3. Educational Reformation Upgrading global education away from rote memorization toward meta-cognition, rigorous skepticism, philosophical literacy, and emotional intelligence in an AI-saturated world. 4. Polycentric Governance Forging binding international treaties, transparent auditing frameworks, and inclusive global regulatory bodies that prevent unchecked corporate and nationalist arms races. Without cultivating deep emotional and philosophical maturity in our leaders, creators, and citizens, no amount of technical alignment mathematics will save us from our own short-sightedness. 04 Conclusion: The Mutual Ascent The symbiotic horizon is neither an inevitable utopia nor a guaranteed apocalypse; it is an ongoing, high-stakes negotiation between human consciousness and machine capability. As we refine our ethical frameworks, institutional resilience, and epistemic discipline, our tools will reflect that heightened wisdom back to us. The Reciprocal Evolution "We do not build AI to replace our humanity. We build AI to reveal what our humanity is truly capable of achieving when unburdened by unnecessary suffering and elevated by relentless truth." Conscious stewardship is our collective mandate. By stepping up to mend our own systemic flaws, we ensure that the dawn of artificial intelligence marks not the twilight of humanity, but the beginning of our greatest evolutionary leap.

JavaScript names are case-sensitive: score and Score are different. 04 Math and comparisons Computers are great at arithmetic, counting, and checking rules. Operator Meaning Example result + Add, or join strings 7 + 2 → 9 - Subtract 7 - 2 → 5 * Multiply 7 * 2 → 14 / Divide 7 / 2 → 3.5 % Remainder after division 7 % 2 → 1 ** Power 3 ** 2 → 9 Order matters: multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction. Use parentheses to make your meaning obvious: (2 + 3) * 4 . Equality and comparisons console.log(5 > 3); // true console.log(5 === 5); // true: same value and type console.log(5 === "5"); // false: number is not text console.log(5 !== 4); // true: not equal Prefer === and !== for equality. The older == can convert types in surprising ways, so beginners should avoid it until they understand coercion. Comparisons include < , > , <= , >= . Logic: combine yes/no answers const hasTicket = true; const isOldEnough = true; console.log(hasTicket && isOldEnough); // AND: both must be true console.log(hasTicket || isOldEnough); // OR: either can be true console.log(!hasTicket); // NOT: flips true/false Think of logic like rules for a game. && means “and”, || means “or”, and ! means “not”. JavaScript’s && and || can return one of their original values, not just true or false ; that shortcut is useful later. Averages and rounding const points = [8, 10, 6]; const total = points[0] + points[1] + points[2]; const average = total / points.length; console.log(Math.round(average)); // 8 Computers use floating-point numbers, so some decimal calculations are tiny bit inexact (for example, 0.1 + 0.2 ). For money, store cents as whole numbers where possible: 199 cents is $1.99. 05 Make decisions Programs choose different actions with conditions. const temperature = 18; if (temperature >= 25) { console.log("Warm day!"); } else if (temperature >= 15) { console.log("A light jacket might help."); } else { console.log("Bundle up!"); } JavaScript checks conditions from top to bottom and runs the first matching branch. Curly braces { } hold the instructions in a block. Indentation is not required by the computer, but it helps people see the structure. Switch for a list of exact choices const day = "Saturday"; switch (day) { case "Saturday": case "Sunday": console.log("Weekend!"); break; default: console.log("School day"); } break stops the switch from continuing into the next case. For many simple choices, if / else is easier to read. Truthy and falsy (a later-level idea) Conditions can use values other than booleans. Values such as 0 , "" , null , undefined , and NaN act like false in a condition; most other values act like true. When learning, explicit checks can be clearer. const nickname = ""; if (nickname) { console.log(`Hi, ${nickname}!`); } else { console.log("No nickname yet."); } 06 Repeat with loops Loops save you from writing the same instruction over and over. Count with a for loop for (let round = 1; round Read it as: start at 1; keep going while the condition is true; add 1 after each turn. The three parts are separated by semicolons. Watch the condition carefully: a mistake can cause an endless loop. Repeat while something is true let energy = 3; while (energy > 0) { console.log("Play!"); energy--; } A while loop checks before each turn. Make sure each turn can eventually make its condition false. Otherwise it may never stop. Loop through a collection const snacks = ["apple", "toast", "yogurt"]; for (const snack of snacks) { console.log(`Pack: ${snack}`); } for...of is a friendly way to visit each item in an array or other iterable. Use break to stop early or continue to skip to the next turn. Loop safety: If a page freezes, a loop might be running forever. Stop the page or close its tab. In your own code, double-check the starting value, stopping condition, and update. 07 Functions: reusable recipes A function groups instructions under a name. Give it inputs; it can return an output. function greet(name) { return `Hello, ${name}!`; } const greeting = greet("Sam"); console.log(greeting); name is a parameter —a named input. "Sam" is an argument —the actual value we pass in. return sends a result back. A function can also do a task without returning a useful value. Function expressions and arrow functions const double = function (number) { return number * 2; }; const triple = (number) => { return number * 3; }; const quadruple = number => number * 4; console.log(double(5), triple(5), quadruple(5)); Arrow functions are a shorter way to write many functions. If the arrow function has one expression, parentheses and braces can be shortened; that expression is returned automatically. Use braces plus return when the steps need more room. Default inputs and input checking function welcome(name = "friend") { return `Welcome, ${name}!`; } function add(a, b) { if (typeof a !== "number" || typeof b !== "number") { return "Please give me two numbers."; } return a + b; } console.log(welcome()); console.log(add(4, 6)); Keep each function focused: one clear job, a helpful name, and predictable inputs and outputs. This makes it easier to test and reuse. 08 Arrays: lists of things Use an array when you have an ordered list of values. const colors = ["teal", "gold", "violet"]; console.log(colors[0]); // "teal"; the first position is 0 console.log(colors.length); // 3 colors.push("coral"); // add to the end colors.pop(); // remove the last item Array positions are called indexes and start at zero. The last valid index is array.length - 1 . A const array can still have items added or removed: the variable still points at the same array. Useful array tools const numbers = [2, 4, 6, 8]; const doubled = numbers.map(number => number * 2); const bigOnes = numbers.filter(number => number >= 6); const found = numbers.find(number => number === 4); const total = numbers.reduce((sum, number) => sum + number, 0); console.log(doubled, bigOnes, found, total); Tool What it does Changes original? map Make a new array by changing each item No filter Make a new array with items that pass a test No find Get the first item that passes a test No reduce Combine items into one answer, such as a total No sort Reorder items (by default, as text) Yes For numbers, sort with a comparison rule: numbers.slice().sort((a, b) => a - b) . slice() makes a copy first, so the original list stays in its old order. Arrays of arrays const seats = [ ["A1", "A2"], ["B1", "B2"] ]; console.log(seats[1][0]); // "B1" 09 Objects: describe a thing An object groups named pieces of information, called properties. const pet = { name: "Pixel", kind: "cat", age: 3, isHungry: false }; console.log(pet.name); // dot notation console.log(pet["kind"]); // bracket notation pet.isHungry = true; Objects are useful when values belong together. A property’s name is its key . Use dot notation when you know the key; use brackets when you have the key in a variable or the name has special characters. Methods: functions that belong to objects const player = { name: "Rin", score: 0, earn(points) { this.score += points; return `${this.name} now has ${this.score} points.`; } }; console.log(player.earn(10)); In this method, this refers to the object that called it. this behaves differently in some kinds of functions; when that feels confusing, use a named parameter or read about arrow-function this rules later. Destructuring and spread const { name, score } = player; // take properties into variables const upgradedPlayer = { ...player, level: 2 }; // copy + add const newColors = [...["blue", "green"], "gold"]; // copy + add Objects are shared by reference: Assigning const otherPet = pet does not make a separate pet. Both names point to the same object. Spreading with { ...pet } makes a shallow copy: nested objects still need more care. JSON: a text format for data const saved = JSON.stringify(pet); // object → JSON text const restored = JSON.parse(saved); // JSON text → object JSON looks similar to JavaScript objects but is stricter: keys and text must use double quotes, and JSON cannot contain functions or undefined . Only parse JSON you trust or handle parse errors. 10 Scope, errors, and debugging Scope is where a name can be used. Debugging is careful detective work. const outside = "I can be used below"; function showMessage() { const inside = "I only exist in this function"; console.log(outside, inside); } showMessage(); // console.log(inside); // Error: inside is out of scope let and const are block-scoped: they live inside the nearest pair of braces where they were declared. Prefer small scopes and avoid reusing the same name for different ideas. Three kinds of problems Syntax error: the code is not written in a way JavaScript understands (perhaps a missing quote or bracket). Runtime error: the code starts, but something goes wrong while it runs. Logic bug: it runs, but gives the wrong answer. A calm debugging checklist Read the whole error message and note the line number. Check spelling, quote marks, brackets, and capitalization. Print intermediate values with console.log() . Test the smallest example that shows the problem. Change one thing, run again, and see whether it helped. Ask: what did I expect, what happened, and what is the first place they differ? function average(a, b) { const total = a + b; console.log("Checking total:", total); // temporary detective clue return total / 2; } console.log(average(8, 10)); Browser Developer Tools offer a debugger. A breakpoint pauses the program on a chosen line so you can inspect variables one step at a time. 11 JavaScript on the web: the DOM HTML describes a page, CSS styles it, and JavaScript can respond and update it. HTML The page structure: headings, buttons, paragraphs, images. CSS The appearance: colors, layout, spacing, motion. JavaScript The behavior: reacting, calculating, updating, communicating. The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser’s live, tree-shaped representation of the page. JavaScript can find an element and change it. // Example HTML:

Create elements instead of building unsafe HTML strings const item = document.createElement("li"); item.textContent = "Learn a new skill"; document.querySelector("ul").append(item); When inserting text from people, use textContent rather than innerHTML . Módulo 0: A Origem de um Superpoder Antes de escrevermos código, precisamos entender o nosso universo. O JavaScript (JS) nasceu em 1995, criado por Brendan Eich na empresa Netscape. Surpreendentemente, ele foi criado em apenas 10 dias! Se a Web fosse uma pessoa: HTML é o esqueleto (a estrutura, ossos). CSS é a roupa e a maquilhagem (o visual, estilo). JavaScript é o cérebro, os músculos e o sistema nervoso (a inteligência, reações e dinamismo). O JavaScript corre diretamente no teu navegador (browser) sem precisar de instalar programas complexos. É a linguagem que faz os jogos web, botões interativos e animações funcionarem. Módulo 1: As Caixas Mágicas (Variáveis e Tipos de Dados) Para programar, precisamos de guardar informação na memória do computador. Fazemos isso usando variáveis . Pensa nelas como caixas onde colamos uma etiqueta com um nome. // Criamos uma caixa chamada 'nomeHeroi' e guardamos um texto (String) let nomeHeroi = "Alex"; // Criamos uma caixa constante (que não muda) chamada 'idade' com um número const idade = 12; // Uma variável lógica (Boolean) que diz se ele está ativo let estaAtivo = true; Tipos de Dados Fundamentais: String : Sequência de caracteres (texto), sempre entre aspas ( "Olá" ). Number : Números inteiros ou decimais ( 12 , 3.14 ). Boolean : Verdadeiro ( true ) ou Falso ( false ). Módulo 2: O Grimório Secreto (A Documentação Oficial) Nenhum herói memoriza todos os feitiços do mundo. Os programadores usam a documentação oficial, sendo a mais famosa a MDN Web Docs (Mozilla Developer Network) . Quando lês a documentação, encontras a sintaxe (como escrever) e os parâmetros (o que a função precisa para funcionar). Por exemplo, a documentação explica que a função console.log() serve para imprimir mensagens na consola do navegador para testes. Módulo 3: Tomando Decisões (Lógica e Condicionais) Um programa inteligente precisa de tomar decisões, tal como tu quando decides se levas guarda-chuva ou não com base no estado do tempo. let nivelPoder = 85; if (nivelPoder >= 90) { console.log("És um Herói de Elite!"); } else if (nivelPoder >= 50) { console.log("Estás no bom caminho, jovem aprendiz!"); } else { console.log("Precisas de treinar mais!"); } Módulo 4: Feitiços Reutilizáveis (Funções) As funções são pequenos blocos de código encapsulados que executam uma tarefa específica. Knowing their names is the easy part; knowing which one answers your question , which flags keep you inside scope, and which two tools only look alike is the job. This manual covers 63 tools across eight families — reconnaissance, web, credentials, wireless, exploitation, sniffing, Active Directory and forensics — with the command that does the work and the mistake that ends an engagement. 63 tool cards 8 families authorised targets only 1 file · no external assets Find a tool All Recon Web Passwords Wireless Exploit Sniff AD Forensics 63 tools · showing all sections 00 Before you touch a keyboard Authorisation, scope, evidence, stop conditions Kali does not make an action legal, and neither does an article. The difference between a penetration test and a crime is a signed scope, a test window and a person who can tell you to stop. Read this page before the tool pages; the commands assume you have already done it. The legal baseline Unauthorised access, interception and modification of systems or data are criminal offences in most jurisdictions, including Portugal (Lei do Cibercrime, Lei n.º 109/2009) and Brazil (Lei n.º 12.737/2012, the Lei Carolina Dieckmann ), and civilly actionable elsewhere. "I was only scanning" is not a defence when the scan was not authorised. This is not legal advice: your lawyer and your client define the contract. The blog has longer arguments about why this matters: Ethical Hacking , Pentesting Society and Interpretation of Attacks and Security Choices . If you have not read them, the short version is: capability is not permission , and the target's safety is part of the job. The six-line contract Parties. Who is authorised to test, on whose behalf, and who signs. Assets. Exact domains, IP ranges, cloud accounts, applications, APIs and accounts in scope — plus an explicit exclusion list. Time. Start, end, blackout periods, rate limits and whether out-of-hours work is allowed. Rules. No denial of service, no social engineering, no data exfiltration beyond proof, no persistence without consent. Stop. A named contact, an out-of-band channel, and the conditions that end the test immediately. Data. Where evidence lives, how it is encrypted, who can read it, when it is destroyed. Build a lab you can break Rehearse on systems that cannot call a lawyer. A host-only virtual network with a deliberately vulnerable target is enough for every command in this manual. Take a snapshot before each drill and revert after it; an un-reverted lab teaches you the wrong lesson about persistence.
