That sentence explains both its strength and its main operational risk: you inherit Debian's package ecosystem and Kali's rolling pace, including fresh tools and fresh bugs. It is a workstation for assessments, not a hardened server and not an invisibility cloak. The old root / toor pair belongs to history. Change the live password immediately, create a non-root account, and never run a browser or office suite as root. Its traffic, user agents, DNS lookups and tool signatures are well known. Stealth is an operational decision, not a distro feature. Not a daily driver. The Penetration Testing Execution Standard and the OWASP Web Security Testing Guide are the standard reference maps; this page is the tool-level companion. 03 Reconnaissance & OSINT Hosts, names, ports, services — and the difference between a lead and a fact Recon is where you earn the rest of the engagement. Passive collection uses public records and third-party sources; active collection sends packets to the target and can be logged, rate-limited or reported. Do passive first, write down every source, and never let a scanner's timeout become a conclusion. 14 cards passive → active scope first Your recon is also evidence about you DNS queries, certificate-transparency lookups, user agents and scan sources are visible to the target and to third parties. Use infrastructure you are authorised to use, not a borrowed VPS, and never assume Tor makes an active scan anonymous — it usually makes it slower and more suspicious. nmap pkg: nmap What it does. The reference port scanner: host discovery, TCP/UDP port states, service and version detection, OS guesses and the NSE scripting engine. It is the tool you use to understand a host, not merely to find an open port. copy sudo nmap -sn 10.10.10.0/24 -oA evidence/scans/discovery sudo nmap -sS -p- --min-rate 1000 -oA evidence/scans/all-tcp 10.10.10.5 sudo nmap -sCV -p 22,80,443 --script safe -oA evidence/scans/services 10.10.10.5 Run it Broad discovery first, then all TCP ports, then a narrow service/script pass. Save with -oA ; a scan without output is a rumour. Use -Pn when ICMP is filtered, -T2 on fragile links, --reason to see why a port is marked open. Avoid -T5 on production or WAN links, --script vuln as a first move (noisy and occasionally disruptive), and UDP sweeps of entire ranges. Closed and filtered are different findings. Instead of masscan or rustscan for speed; nmap for truth. -sT works without raw sockets but is more connection-heavy; -sS is the usual choice when you have root. masscan pkg: masscan What it does. An asynchronous TCP port scanner with its own userland network stack. It trades accuracy and depth for raw speed across very large address ranges: no service detection, no scripts, no OS fingerprinting. copy sudo masscan -p1-65535 10.10.10.0/24 --rate=1000 \ --exclude 10.10.10.1 -oL evidence/scans/masscan.lst Run it Only on ranges you own or are authorised to test. Start at --rate 1000 , watch for packet loss, then verify every hit with nmap. Add --wait 3 so late replies are not lost. Avoid Internet-wide scans, rates that saturate a shared uplink, and treating a masscan miss as "closed". Its stack can be less reliable than the kernel's, especially behind NAT or stateful firewalls. Instead of Use it to find candidates across /16s and /8s; hand each live host to nmap. For a single host or a /24, rustscan is usually more convenient and nmap alone is already fast enough. rustscan pkg: rustscan What it does. Finds open TCP ports quickly, then automatically hands the open ports to nmap for service and script detection. Think of it as a fast front door with nmap waiting inside. copy rustscan -a 10.10.10.5 --ulimit 5000 -- -sV -sC -oA evidence/scans/rustscan Run it Everything after -- is passed to nmap. Raise --ulimit only on a machine you control. Use -b to tune batch size and --scan-order random to reduce obvious sequential patterns. Avoid Assuming its result is more accurate than nmap. It is a convenience wrapper; the nmap pass is what produces the evidence. Do not run high concurrency through a fragile VPN or IDS-heavy path. Instead of Use rustscan for a quick "which ports are open?" on one host; nmap directly when you need careful timing or complex NSE; masscan for enormous ranges. arp-scan pkg: arp-scan What it does. Discovers hosts on the local Layer-2 segment using ARP requests. Because ARP is not routed, it is authoritative only for the subnet you are plugged into — and it often finds devices that ignore ICMP. copy sudo arp-scan -I eth0 --localnet --retry 2 Run it Use --localnet or an explicit CIDR, and confirm the interface with ip -brief addr . Repeat once to catch sleeping devices. The vendor column comes from the MAC OUI and is a hint, not proof. Avoid Using it to infer hosts behind a router; ARP does not cross L3 boundaries. Do not confuse a silent host with an absent one — some stacks rate-limit ARP replies. Instead of nmap -sn is better for routed discovery; arp-scan is better for the local wire and for finding quiet appliances. Compare both before declaring a subnet empty. dnsrecon pkg: dnsrecon What it does. Enumerates DNS records and infrastructure: standard record types, zone-transfer attempts, SRV records, cache snooping and dictionary-based subdomain brute force. It is the quick, scriptable DNS check before a heavier mapping tool. copy dnsrecon -d example.com -t std --json evidence/recon/dnsrecon.json dnsrecon -d example.com -t brt \ -D /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt Run it Start with -t std , then targeted -t axfr against each authoritative name server. Brute force only with permission and a sensible wordlist; use --threads conservatively so you do not poison your own resolver. Avoid Treating NXDOMAIN as proof a name does not exist (wildcards and split-horizon DNS exist), and brute-forcing a third-party domain you merely found in a certificate. Instead of dnsenum adds scraping and whois; fierce is lighter and focuses on non-contiguous IP space; amass is the deep mapping tool. dnsrecon is the fast first pass. dnsenum pkg: dnsenum What it does. A Perl-era DNS enumeration script: record lookups, zone-transfer attempts, subdomain brute force, reverse lookups and optional search-engine scraping. It remains useful because its output is compact and its zone-transfer routine is blunt. copy dnsenum --enum example.com \ -f /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt -r Run it Use --enum as the shortcut and -r for recursive brute force. Save the terminal output; dnsenum's file output is less structured than dnsrecon's JSON. Avoid Relying on its Google scraping — search providers block or change formats constantly. Do not run recursion without a time limit; it can expand quickly. Instead of Prefer dnsrecon for clean JSON and current record types, or amass for a serious map. Keep dnsenum for a quick second opinion or an environment where it is already installed. fierce pkg: fierce What it does. A focused DNS reconnaissance tool for finding hosts in non-contiguous IP space: it resolves names, tests zone transfers, detects wildcards and brute-forces subdomains with a small, fast workflow. copy fierce --domain example.com \ --subdomains /usr/share/seclists/Discovery/DNS/subdomains-top1million-5000.txt Run it Read the wildcard warning: if every random name resolves, brute-force results are meaningless until you filter the wildcard address. Keep the default timeouts for public DNS and raise them only in a lab. Avoid Using it as an attack tool — it is a resolver and a mapper. It will not find names that only exist in internal DNS, and it cannot see hosts that never appear in DNS. Instead of Faster to type than amass and cleaner than dnsenum for a single domain. Choose amass when you need certificates, ASNs, API sources and a graph; choose fierce for a five-minute answer. whois pkg: whois What it does. Queries the registration system for a domain, IP or ASN: registrar, creation and expiry dates, name servers, registrant organisation (when not redacted) and abuse contacts. RDAP is the modern JSON successor. copy whois example.com whois -h whois.iana.org example.com curl -s https://rdap.org/domain/example.com | jq '.events, .nameservers' Run it Query the authoritative registry for the TLD, then the registrar. Exemplo para Crianças e Adultos: O Manuel é professor de matemática e durante uma das suas aulas, um qualquer aluno está distraído a falar com outro aluno. Nisto eles riem-se e o professor repára. Na perspectiva puramente educativa (sabendo que a vida serve somente para aprender e ensinar, pois só assim podemos todos melhorar) existe um problema na aula que o professor está a dirigir. Para curiosidade de quem ensina, faz o uso do que todos os alunos podem fazer e então, pergunta aos alunos, qual a razão de se estarem a rir. Na consideração que se estavam a rir de uma aluna que estava a dormir, a razão de se rirem, é válida. Por outro lado caso a razão de se rirem estivesse relacionado com algo que não faz parte daquela aula, teriamos de aplicar justiça. Sabendo que o objectivo de aplicar uma punição tem como Finalidade Ensinar e Disciplinar os alunos a estarem mais atentos ao conteúdo da disciplina de matemática, o professor pede aos alunos para irem ao quadro, resolver um problema matemático. Resolver problemas matemáticos a partir do conhecimento que têm.
